headline: Power BI Data Modelling: Star Schema Beats Flat Tables for Performance
summary: Learn why relationships and schemas are crucial for efficient Power BI data models, moving beyond simple flat tables to optimize performance and readability.
details: The core of any Power BI report is its data model, not just the visuals. A flat table, while simple, becomes inefficient and unable to support multiple business processes, as discovered when trying to compare actuals vs. budget.

A star schema, with a central fact table and surrounding dimension tables, is optimized for Power BI's VertiPaq engine, offering speed and clarity. Snowflake schemas further normalize dimensions but can add complexity.

Distinguish between facts (events, like sales amounts) and dimensions (attributes, like customer names). Each fact table needs a defined grain – a clear description of what a row represents – to avoid issues like double-counting revenue.

Relationships in Power BI are filter paths, not merges. They should almost always be one-to-many. Many-to-many relationships typically require a bridge table, and role-playing dates (like order vs. ship dates) use USERELATIONSHIP.
Prefer single-direction filtering to maintain performance and avoid complex filter paths. Bidirectional filtering can be convenient but often complicates row-level security and performance.

Power Query's Merge Queries offer various join kinds (Left/Right/Full Outer, Inner, Anti) for data transformation. Merges run at refresh time and add columns, while relationships are evaluated at query time with minimal cost.

Avoid merging dimensions directly into fact tables to save building relationships. This can recreate the problems of a flat table. Instead, merge dimensions into cleaner dimensions and use relationships for connections.

A robust default Power BI model includes a star schema, one-to-many relationships, a proper DimDate table, and single-direction filtering. While it takes a few extra hours upfront, it saves significant time and effort later.

headline_marked: iOS 27 bug [[temporarily freezes]] iPhones with specific swipe sequence
headline: iOS 27 bug temporarily freezes iPhones with specific swipe sequence
summary: A bug in iOS 27 can cause iPhones to freeze when swiping down the Notification Center and Control Center in quick succession. A force restart is required to fix it.
details: A newly discovered bug in iOS 27 has been reported to temporarily freeze iPhones. The issue occurs when users perform a specific sequence of swipes, leading to an unresponsive device.

The bug is triggered by swiping down the Notification Center and then the Control Center in rapid succession. This action causes interface elements to get stuck at the top of the screen, preventing any further input.
While alarming, the bug does not permanently damage the iPhone. Users can resolve the freeze by performing a force restart, a standard troubleshooting step for many device issues.

To force restart a frozen iPhone, users must quickly press and release the volume up button, then do the same for the volume down button. Immediately after, press and hold the side button until the Apple logo appears.
Apple is expected to release a fix for this iOS 27 bug in a future software update. In the meantime, users are advised to be aware of the trigger and know how to perform a force restart.
